messages.subject: GGIR sustainability
parts:
Dear GGIR users,

I am receiving requests for help and additional package functionality
on a weekly basis. It is great to see that people are so excited about
the package, but my time is limited. The package is released under the
open source license agreement, which does not mean that I have an
obligation to help you or that if I help you my time is for free.

Therefore, the future of GGIR depends on the willingness of me or
other people to continue developing and maintaining GGIR. This does
not only relate to desired functional improvements with clear
scientific impacts, but also relates to general investment in the
software quality and sustainability: readability of the code to enable
future developers to make improvements, speed of the code,
implementation of a much needed code test environment, more efficient
storage of the milestone data, better documentation, and possibly
various other aspects. None of these enhancement activities will
result in a scientific publication but if these activities are not
done the code is at risk of becoming obsolete in the upcoming
decade(s). Any piece of scientific software has this problem.

Ideally, there needs to be a community of GGIR developers in which
anyone is replaceable, including myself. For most computer scientists
this type of work is boring because the focus is not on innovation but
on sustainability and quality control. So, the only way to realise all
this is if you as GGIR end-users and stakeholders make a direct
investment. For example:
- Add a budget for a scientific programmer in your next grant
application to review and improve the GGIR code.
- Add a budget for a research assistant/technician in your next grant
application to learn GGIR and then educate other GGIR users via
courses/workshops, and respond to help requests on this email list.
- When you appoint your next student to develop new analytical methods
encourage them to re-use my code where possible instead of
re-inventing the wheel and starting from scratch. It took me six years
to develop GGIR to what it is today and I am sure you could safe
yourself a lot of time if you did at least consider re-using some of
the code.
- Don’t keep the developments to yourself but share them on github and
communicate what you are doing on this e-mail list such that efforts
can be coordinated. A GitHub repo of the current version of GGIR is
here, https://github.com/ucl-cls/mcs-acc, which is hosted by UCL in
London.

If you feel that you still need my involvement, then please get in
touch and we could explore commercial consultancy options, although my
time is limited. Finally, I would like to encourage scientists based
in The Netherlands to apply for funding at my employer:
www.esciencecenter.nl.

With kind regards,

Vincent van Hees
